"""Agentic Retrieval From Scratch — stage 2: Ten million documents, and the index that is a decision.

Ten million documents are a number before they are a system, and this stage is
the arithmetic that number forces. Before anything can be retrieved, the corpus
is an estate — clauses, terms, postings, vectors, and the bytes all of it weighs
— and the estate's own numbers are the only numbers that matter. `corpus.SCALE`
is the customer's answer to how big their corpus is, and every figure a plan
reports is that scale's arithmetic, recomputed rather than believed.

The estate does not fit as one flat index, and not every plan fits its budget. A
flat index pays one dictionary and every vector, and a query scans all of it.
Sharding by document pays a dictionary per shard and scans only its own shard:
memory bought with memory, spent on the scan. A two-tier layout keeps the
dictionary whole and pays vectors only for the hot clauses, so memory drops and
a query still touches the hot tier whatever it scans. A plan is therefore a
search — over the layouts and the shard counts, keep what the memory budget and
the scan budget both allow, and answer the smallest memory, ties by the order
`LAYOUTS` spells them and then fewest shards.

What happens when nothing fits is the point of the stage. A plan that cannot pay
is not promised and not quietly rounded down: it is returned as
`verdict = "refused"`, with the reason and the offending number, because the
customer is entitled to know which constraint broke and by how much. Memory is
rounded *up* for the same reason — a plan that rounds down is a plan that does
not fit. Both prices are the customer's: indexing is charged per million
postings, a query per million clauses scanned, so the scan a layout buys is also
the cost a query pays.

    LAYOUTS                              the three layouts a plan may choose, in order
    PLAN_PROBLEMS                        the closed vocabulary a refusal is spelled in
    PLAN_KEYS                            the nine fields of a plan, in order
    POSTING_BYTES                        the bytes one posting takes
    TERM_BYTES                           the bytes one dictionary term takes
    VECTOR_BYTES                         the bytes one vector component takes
    BYTES_PER_MB                         the bytes in one megabyte
    POSTINGS_PER_CLAUSE                  the postings one clause contributes
    SCAN_BUDGET_BP                       the widest scan a query may make, in basis points
    MAX_SHARDS                           the most shards a plan may be cut into
    INDEX_CENTS_PER_MILLION_POSTINGS     what a million postings cost to index
    QUERY_CENTS_PER_MILLION_SCANNED      what a million clauses scanned cost to query
    PlanError                            the shape this stage will not accept
    weigh(scale)                         -> the estate's flat figures, as a dict
    bytes_of(layout, shards, scale)      -> the bytes that layout holds, in total
    scan_of(layout, shards, scale)       -> the basis points of the estate a query scans
    plan(scale, budget_mb)               -> PLAN_KEYS, the cheapest layout that pays
    explain(plan)                        -> the (claim, number) pairs the plan rests on

DESIGN DECISION — why is memory rounded up rather than to the nearest megabyte?
Because a plan is a promise about what will fit, and a promise rounded down is
a promise the machine cannot keep. `memory_mb` is the ceiling of the estate's
bytes over a megabyte, so a plan whose true weight is 5997 megabytes and a
fraction is reported as 5997 and only fits a budget of 5997 or more. A caller
who rounds down saves a megabyte on paper and watches the index spill in
production; the arithmetic here is deliberately unkind.

DESIGN DECISION — why does sharding pay a dictionary per shard?
Because that is the price of sharding and this stage refuses to hide it. A
sharded index scans only its own shard, which is what the scan budget wants, but
each shard needs its own term dictionary to answer a query at all, and the plan
shows the whole bill rather than a per-shard average a reader would have to
multiply back out. The tension is the design: more shards buy a narrower scan
and cost more memory, so the plan searches rather than assumes.

DESIGN DECISION — why is the layout chosen by memory while the scan is a
separate budget?
Because the two are different promises to different people. Memory is what the
customer buys once; the scan is what every query pays forever. A layout that
holds the estate but scans too wide is not a cheaper plan, it is a plan whose
query budget is broken, so both constraints are applied and a plan that fails
either is not kept. Keeping the scan in basis points means query cost is priced
by the same fraction that decides the plan.

DESIGN DECISION — why is a plan that does not fit returned rather than raised?
Because a plan that cannot pay is still a decision, and the useful part of it is
*why*. Raising would say "no" and hide which of the two budgets broke and by how
much; returning `verdict = "refused"` with `("over-budget", memory_mb)` or

against a number rather than a mood. Only a shape that cannot be a plan at all —
no budget, an estate missing its numbers — raises, because there is nothing to
decide about it.

DESIGN DECISION — why does the search vary the shard count at all?
Because the shard count is the one dial that trades the two budgets against each
other, and leaving it at one would decide the question this stage exists to
answer. `plan` walks every layout cut `1..MAX_SHARDS` ways, keeps only the plans
that pay both budgets, and answers the smallest memory; `MAX_SHARDS` is the
point past which sharding has stopped being worth its dictionaries.

    raise NotImplementedError("stage 2: implement bytes_of()")

"""Agentic Retrieval From Scratch — stage 3: Two scorers, and the fusion that has to beat both.

The customer's library already holds an analyzer, an inverse document frequency and a
unit-scaled vector, and it will not tell you which of the three modes to run: that is
the decision this stage exists to make. So the stage builds one index over the chunks
stage 1 produced, scores those chunks two different ways, fuses the two rankings, and
then answers the only question that matters — *which mode does the customer's own
labelled evaluation set prefer?* — as data rather than as an opinion about embeddings.

The index is the stage's own record: it chunks every document with stage 1's chunker,
analyzes each chunk's text once, embeds each chunk's text once, and keeps the per-chunk
term counts, the chunk lengths, the term-to-chunk postings and the vectors. A hit is
not a number: it is the chunk, the score and the arithmetic that produced the score, so
a reader can recompute every ranking the index ever answers. That is the whole point of
a fixed point — a score whose explanation is exactly the terms that make it.

Two scorers, one vocabulary. BM25 is lexical: an inverse document frequency in basis
points multiplied by a term frequency saturated and length-normalised, all in integers,
so a rare term matters more, a repeated term matters less and less, and a long clause is
not punished for being long. Dense is a plain dot product: the library hands back
vectors of the same scale, so a similarity needs no division, no square root and no
float anywhere. Fusion is reciprocal rank fusion — ranks, not scores, because two
scorers have two different scales and only their order is comparable — and it is the
mode that has to beat both.

The last half is the measurement. `measure` runs a mode over the customer's sixteen
labelled questions and answers how many of them were fully retrieved, what share of the
expected clauses came back, and which questions missed. `pick` runs all three, names
the best and — this is the stage's verdict — says `"no-difference"` when the best beats
the runner-up by less than `NO_DIFFERENCE_BP`, because a mode that is not demonstrably
better is not better.

    MEASURE_KEYS                                 the four fields of a measurement, in order
    SEARCH_MODES                                 the three modes a search may run in
    BM25_K1_BP                                   the BM25 term-saturation fixed point
    BM25_B_BP                                    the BM25 length-normalisation fixed point
    RRF_K                                        the reciprocal rank fusion constant
    SCORE_SCALE                                  the fixed point a whole score is written in
    NO_DIFFERENCE_BP                             the gap below which two modes are the same
    Index                                        the chunks, their counts, their vectors and the postings
    Index.build(corpus)                          -> the index over every chunk of every document
    Index.corpus                                 the corpus this index was built from
    Index.chunks                                 every chunk of every document, in document order
    Index.of(chunk_id)                           -> the chunk record, or None
    Index.terms(text)                            -> the corpus's analyzer, and one ask it made
    Index.vector(text)                           -> the corpus's embedder, and one ask it made
    Index.lexical(query, limit)                  -> the BM25 ranking of hits
    Index.dense(query, limit)                    -> the dot-product ranking of hits
    Index.fused(query, limit)                    -> the fusion of this index's two rankings
    Index.analysis()                             -> the index's own counts
    bm25(index, query, limit)                    -> the lexical ranking of hits
    dense(index, query, limit)                   -> the dense ranking of hits
    fuse(lexical, dense, limit)                  -> the fused ranking of hits
    search(index, query, limit, mode)            -> the ranking the mode asked for
    measure(index, questions, limit, mode)       -> MEASURE_KEYS over the labelled set

Because a ranking nobody can recompute is a ranking nobody can check. A score is a
number the index chose, and the only honest defence of it is the terms that produced
it: `why` is a tuple of `(name, contribution)` pairs, sorted by name, and the score is
their sum. A reader, a check or a later stage can add them up and get the score back —

measured against, the fusion's two ranks and the reciprocal-rank sum. A score with no
explanation is the first place a retrieval system starts lying.

DESIGN DECISION — why a fixed point instead of a float?
Because this course has no float and no logarithm anywhere, and a similarity has to be
an integer to be compared exactly. So a ratio is basis points, the BM25 parameters are
fixed points (`BM25_K1_BP = 120` is `k1` of one and two tenths), and the score is

places to keep straight instead of one. The index is what the corpus was asked, so it is

Because "hybrid is better" is a claim about embeddings, and the customer paid for the

answer to "which of the three" is sometimes "it does not matter".

"""Agentic Retrieval From Scratch — stage 4: The reranker that must earn its place.

answered with a measurement rather than an opinion. This stage is the next thing
somebody will ask for, and it is asked for the same way: a reranker is added, and
then somebody has to say whether it helped. The honest answer is not "the reranker
is better" — it is a comparison of two measurements of the *same* questions over
the *same* candidate set, and a threshold below which the difference is not a
difference at all. A reranker that cannot clear that threshold is removed, and
saying so is this stage's output.

The reranker itself is deliberately small and deliberately explainable. It never
looks at the fusion's score; it looks at the query and at the chunk, and it writes
down what it saw: how much of the query the chunk covers, how tightly the query's
terms sit together inside it, and whether the clause is a top-level one. Those
three numbers are the hit's `signals`, sorted by name, and the score is a fixed
point arithmetic over them and nothing else — so a reader who doubts a rank can
recompute it from the tuple that was printed beside it, and a check can too.

The measurement is stage 3's, not this stage's: `before` is literally stage 3's
`measure(..., "hybrid")`, and `after` is the same counting over the same questions
with the reranker in the same place the fusion left it. The only number this stage
adds is their difference, and the only judgement is where that difference falls
against `NOISE_BP` — under it the change is noise, at or above it the reranker has
earned its place. `keep` is that verdict spelled as a decision for the person who
has to decide.

    COMPARE_KEYS         the four fields of the verdict, in order
    COVERAGE_WEIGHT      what the coverage carries of a rerank score, out of WEIGHT_TOTAL
    PROXIMITY_WEIGHT     what the proximity carries of it
    WEIGHT_TOTAL         what the two weights add up to
    PROXIMITY_WINDOW     how near another distinct query term has to be, in positions
    LEVEL_BONUS_BP       what a top-level clause's own level is worth, in basis points
    NOISE_BP             a coverage gain below this many basis points is noise
    rerank(index, query, hits, limit)   -> the hits, rescored and reordered
    compare(index, questions, limit)    -> COMPARE_KEYS: hybrid against hybrid-reranked

reorder that page, and a reordering of a fixed set cannot change `hit_bp` — the
measurement would come back identical every time and the stage would be theatre.

something better to the top, so `compare` hands it the *whole* fused ranking (the
same `search`, at the index's own size) and cuts the result to the caller's limit.

caller asked for, which is why the comparison is about the reranker and not about
how deep somebody fetched.

"""Agentic Retrieval From Scratch — stage 6: The critique of what came back.

chunk from a document the estate has already replaced, a chunk whose own
cross-reference points at a clause its document never held, a chunk that disagrees
with another chunk in the same answer about the same subject, and a chunk with
nothing to do with the question are each named here — with the offender they are
against — before stage 7 is allowed to write a sentence out of any of them. The
verdict is data: one row per chunk that came back, in the order it came back, so the
pipeline that follows is held to what it retrieved rather than to what it says about
itself.

The order is the whole decision. Supersession is a fact about the document, a dangling
reference is a fact about the chunk's own text, a conflict is a fact about the other
chunks that came back with it, and only then is the question's own vocabulary
consulted. A chunk that is true of more than one of those is named by the first thing
true of it in `VERDICT_ORDER` and never by a later one, because a caller reading
`stale` must not be told `off-topic` instead.

    CRITIQUE_KEYS      the four fields of one row: chunk, verdict, reason, against
    CRITIQUE_VERDICTS  the closed vocabulary a verdict is drawn from
    VERDICT_ORDER      the priority the verdicts are decided in, first true wins
    critique           chunks, query, corpus → one row per chunk, in input order
    survivors          the `supported` chunk ids, in the order the rows arrived
    by_verdict         every verdict of the vocabulary → its chunk ids, sorted

`if`s written where they happen to fall? Because the order *is* this stage's answer to
the item it exists for: a chunk can be stale and off-topic at once, and which of the
two the caller is told is a decision, not an accident of how the comparisons were
laid out. `VERDICT_ORDER` is that decision written down and pinned, so a later
refactor that reorders the checks fails rather than silently changing a verdict.

DESIGN DECISION — why is a conflict measured against the chunk's *input* rather than
against the whole corpus? Because the critique is about what came back for *this*
question. Two clauses of the estate may share a subject and never both be retrieved,
and calling that a conflict would make every answer conflict with documents that are
not in it. The subject tag is the library's own label, but the disagreement is a fact
only about the chunks this call was handed.

`reason`? Because a reason is for a person and the offender is data: the stages that
follow must know what a chunk was judged against — the superseding document, the
missing clause, the other chunk — without parsing a sentence. A row that names its
offender only in its `reason` is a row nothing downstream can act on.

clause index rather than against the chunks that came back? Because the fault is the
chunk's, not the retrieval's: a clause its document never held is broken text, while a
clause the document holds and the retrieval merely missed is a retrieval miss, which

"""Agentic Retrieval From Scratch — stage 7: Grounded or abstain, and never a claim without a citation.

answer. The question was made unambiguous, chunks were ranked, a reranker earned
or lost its place, and stage 6 named every chunk that is stale, off-topic, in
conflict or unresolvable. What comes back from all of that is a list of
survivors, and this stage is the only one that turns survivals into something a
customer may read: an answer made of claims, each one tied to the span it came
from, or an abstention that says why it has nothing to say. There is no third
shape, and a scanner proves it.

The shape of an answer is the decision. The pipeline may quote and may not
invent, so a claim's `text` is the chunk's own text verbatim and its `cite` is
that chunk's id, and the answer's `citations` are those ids in the order the
claims are in — a citation list that has been sorted is a citation list that no
longer says which claim came from where. An answer that cannot do that does not
answer at all: `ABSTENTIONS` is a closed vocabulary of four reasons, and the
first one true of the run is the one reported, so two runs over one input never
disagree about why the pipeline stayed silent.

Grounding is the number that decides the commonest of those four. It is the share
of the query's **distinct** analyzed terms that the surviving chunks' texts
actually carry, in basis points — measured rather than felt, and measured over
the chunks that survived rather than over everything that was retrieved, because
the question is whether what the pipeline is about to quote can answer what was
asked. The comparison is *below* the minimum, so a run exactly at the minimum is
grounded: the threshold is a floor, and the reason a refusal prints names both
numbers so that an auditor can recompute the verdict instead of trusting it.

The scanner is the other half, and it is deliberately not a method of the answer.
`check_citations` reads **any** answer — one this stage built, one a caller typed,
one a later stage mangled — and reports what is wrong with it as data: a claim
whose cite is empty or absent from the citation list, a citation the input chunks
do not hold, a citation naming a clause the document prints twice, and an
abstention that carries claims anyway. `()` is what a clean answer scans to, and
that is the proof that the third shape does not exist.

    CLAIM_KEYS                                   the two fields of a claim, in order
    ANSWER_KEYS                                  the six fields of an answer, in order
    ABSTENTIONS                                  the four reasons an answer abstains for, in precedence order
    CITATION_PROBLEMS                            the four faults a scanner reports, in the order it reports them

to 10 after them, need to walk back from a sentence to the clause it came from,
and the only way that walk exists is if the drawing of the sentence — the claim's
`text` — is the span's own words rather than a paraphrase of them. Nothing in
this stage writes a word: a claim quotes a chunk and cites it, `citations` is
nothing but those ids in claim order, and an answer that would have to invent a
sentence to exist abstains instead. That is also why the claims are one per
surviving chunk rather than one per expected id: this stage answers from what
survived the critique, not from what the evaluation set believes.

Because a partial answer is a false one. A pipeline that quotes the two clauses
it could ground and silently drops the third has told the customer that the third
does not exist, and there is no way for a reader to tell that apart from a
complete answer. So an answer is all of the survivors or none of them: the four
reasons in `ABSTENTIONS` are the only four things that can be true, they are
tested in the order they are written, and the reason is data the caller can
branch on rather than a sentence this stage made up.

"""Agentic Retrieval From Scratch — stage 8: The loop that must terminate, priced every round.

Seven stages of retrieval, each one a single pass: a document becomes citable
chunks, chunks become an index, the index answers a query twice and fuses the
two, a reranker reorders what came back, a question is made unambiguous before
it is asked, what came back is critiqued with the offender named, and the
answer is claims tied to spans or an abstention with a reason. Every one of
those is a function of its inputs. This stage is the first one that *asks
again*, and asking again is where a pipeline stops being a function and becomes
a loop — which is to say, a thing that can also fail by never finishing.

The loop is the build-5 skill of the roadmap: search, critique what came back,
rewrite the query, search again. What makes it a stage rather than a `while`
statement is that it is bounded twice and priced every round. The bound is the
caller's: a budget in cents and a cap on how many rewrites are allowed. The
price is the customer's: each round charges the customer's own meter for the
retrieval, the rerank, the critique and the generation it performed, and the
cents a round reports is the *meter's own delta* for that round rather than
this stage's belief about what it should have cost. A loop that cannot say what
it spent is a loop that cannot be run under a budget at all.

The ways a round can end the loop are decisions, not accidents, and each is a
row of data rather than an exception: the answer is not an abstention
(`answered`), the rewrite would search a query already searched (`repeat`), the
rewrites allowed are used up (`round-cap`), or the next round would spend past
the budget (`budget`). An abstention that stops the loop reports itself
(`abstained`) with the answer's own reason, so the honest "I could not ground
this" is never replaced by a mechanical one.

    ROUND_KEYS          the six fields of one round, in order
    LOOP_KEYS           the six fields of the loop's own answer, in order
    STOPS               the closed vocabulary of what stopped the loop
    RETRIEVE_UNITS      units of retrieval a round charges the meter
    RERANK_UNITS        units of reranking a round charges the meter
    CRITIQUE_UNITS      units of critique a round charges the meter
    GENERATE_UNITS      units of generation a round charges the meter
    DEFAULT_LIMIT       the retrieval width this course treats as the default
    ask(index, corpus, meter, question, tick, limit, budget_cents, round_cap)
                        -> LOOP_KEYS, the rounds it ran and why it stopped
    rounds_of(loop)     -> the rounds a loop ran, in the order it ran them

DESIGN DECISION — why is the budget checked before the round rather than after
it?
Because a budget is a promise about what this loop will spend, and a check
after the call is a check that has already broken it. A round's price is
knowable before the round runs — the customer's own table prices the four
charges a round makes — so the loop compares what it has spent plus that price
against the budget and refuses to run a round whose whole cost would leave the
meter above what the caller allowed. The number a stop reports is therefore the
number it would have spent, which is the number the caller needs to decide
whether to raise the budget or narrow the loop.

DESIGN DECISION — why is a round's cost the meter's delta rather than the sum
this stage can compute for itself?
Because a sum this stage computes is a belief, and the objects here are the
customer's. The price table could change, a round could charge more than the
four calls it names, and a stage that reported its own arithmetic would keep
agreeing with itself while disagreeing with the ledger. The meter keeps the
log; the delta between its total before the round and its total after is the
one number that cannot be wrong about what was spent, and a round's own
`cost_cents` is exactly that delta.

DESIGN DECISION — why does a rewrite that changes nothing end the loop instead
of being tried again?
Because a loop whose next query is the query it just searched is a loop that
does not terminate for a reason, and the question's own abstention is a better
answer than an unbounded search. On the customer's own question a rewrite with
no fix yields the text unchanged: there is nothing left to rewrite, so the loop
stops on the abstention it already holds and reports the answer's own reason.
Once a rewrite has been applied, a rewrite that lands on a query the loop has
already searched is the same failure differently named, and it stops as
`repeat`.

DESIGN DECISION — why is the cap counted in rewrites rather than in rounds?
Because the thing that can grow without bound is the rewriting, not the
searching. Counting rounds would make the first search cost a rewrite, so every
question would pay one even when it never needed rewriting; counting rewrites
means the customer's own question is always tried once and only the attempts to
improve it are capped. The arithmetic is then exact — at most `round_cap`
rewrites, so at most `round_cap + 1` rounds — and a cap that is hit is named as
what it is rather than discovered as a timeout.

DESIGN DECISION — why is a round's record rebuilt rather than the question
reused?
Because what changes between rounds is the text, and nothing else. The rewriter
needs the question's own `expected` and `conversation` to know what a pronoun
refers to and what a two-hop question wants, so the record handed to it carries
those fields untouched and only the text advanced; a rewritten query that lost
the question's expectations would be rewritten against nothing and answered
against nothing.

TODO: implement `ask` and `rounds_of` in this file: the budgeted loop that
retrieves, reranks, critiques and answers a round at a time, rewrites once per
abstention, charges the customer's meter for every call, and names the one
thing that stopped it.
"""

import corpus
import meter

import stage_03
import stage_04
import stage_05
import stage_06
import stage_07

ROUND_KEYS = ("round", "query", "rewrites", "retrieved", "survivors", "cost_cents")

LOOP_KEYS = ("question", "answer", "rounds", "cost_cents", "stopped", "reason")

STOPS = ("answered", "abstained", "budget", "round-cap", "repeat")

RETRIEVE_UNITS = 1

RERANK_UNITS = 1

CRITIQUE_UNITS = 1

GENERATE_UNITS = 1

DEFAULT_LIMIT = 5


def ask(index, corpus, meter, question, tick, limit, budget_cents, round_cap):
    """Run the budgeted loop over one question and answer what it did.

    Round 0 searches the question's own text; every later round searches the text

    reranks it, critiques it and answers from the survivors, charging the
    customer's meter one retrieval, one rerank, one critique and one generation,
    and reporting the meter's own delta as the round's `cost_cents`.

    The budget is checked before each round: a round whose price would leave the
    meter above `budget_cents` is not run, and the loop stops `budget` naming the
    total it would have reached and the budget. An answer that is not an
    abstention stops the loop `answered`; an abstention rewrites once and
    continues, until a query already searched stops it `repeat`, the `round_cap`
    rewrites allowed stop it `round-cap`, or nothing is left to rewrite and it
    stops `abstained` with the answer's own reason. Shapes this stage cannot
    accept — a question that is not a `QUESTION_KEYS` record, a limit, tick,
    budget or cap that is not a whole number — raise, naming the offender.
    """

def rounds_of(loop):
    """The rounds a loop ran, in the order it ran them.

    A `LOOP_KEYS` record carries its rounds; anything that is not one raises,
    naming what arrived.
    """
    raise NotImplementedError("stage 8: implement rounds_of()")
files.stage_09.py:
"""Agentic Retrieval From Scratch — stage 9: What the checking cost, against the naive answer.

The last stage before the customer's own failures. A pipeline that checks itself
has to be worth what the checking cost, and the null hypothesis it has to beat is
the pipeline nobody would write a book about: retrieve the hybrid top `limit` and
answer from all of it. No critique, no rewrite, no abstention — the naive row
cannot abstain, because there was never a gate for it to fail, so its `answered`
is every question it was shown.

Against it stands the loop of stage 8, priced round by round out of the meter's own
log. The checked row's `answered` is the questions it did not abstain on, and its
coverage is measured over what its answers cite: an abstention cites nothing, which
is the honest way for checking to lose coverage it never had.

Nothing here is a model of the customer's business. The two rows are counts of
questions and basis points of coverage, and the verdict between them is a
comparison of one number against another with the noise floor the plan pinned.
`where_it_lost` is the part an average would have hidden — the questions where the
checked pipeline paid more and handed over no more of what was expected.

The surface:

    BASELINE_KEYS         one row of the comparison: its kind, its cents, its answers,
                          its coverage
    ROLLUP_KEYS           the two rows added up: cost, answers, cents per answer, and
                          the two deltas
    MIN_WORTH_IT_GAIN_BP  the coverage gain, in basis points, that checking has to
                          reach to have paid for itself
    price                 both pipelines over one question set, the naive row first,
                          each row priced by the meter it was handed
    rollup                the two rows summed, with `None` cents per answer when
                          nothing was answered
    where_it_lost         the questions the checked pipeline paid more for and brought
                          no more expected ids to the customer
    worth_it              the verdict: worth it, not worth it, or inside the noise

DESIGN DECISION — what is the null hypothesis, and who answers from it?

The naive pipeline is the one without a checking stage: one hybrid retrieval at
`limit`, and one generation that quotes everything the retrieval handed back. It
has no critique to consult, so it never abstains, and no rewrite, so it retrieves
once per question. Its `answered` is therefore `len(questions)` by construction
rather than by luck: an abstention would be a gate it does not have.

DESIGN DECISION — whose number is a row's cost?

The meter's. A row reads `Meter.total_cents()` before it starts and subtracts it
when it is done, so a row's cost is the delta the ledger shows and not an
arithmetic the stage believes. The rows run in the order the contract pins — naive
first, checked second — because a delta means one thing only while the charges are
contiguous.

DESIGN DECISION — what is coverage measured over, row by row?

Stage 3's rule, over the ids each row brings to the customer: expected ids brought
over every expected id, in basis points. The naive row brings what it retrieved —
it has nothing else — and the checked row brings what its answers cite, which is
nothing at all on an abstention. The two numbers are deliberately not the same
measurement: the checked row is charged for the ids it was willing to stand behind.

DESIGN DECISION — where does the tick come from, when `price` is handed no clock?

The question's own position in the list the caller supplied: one call, one tick. A
run is a function of the questions' order — the only order this course has — and the
meter's log can still say which question paid rather than just how much a run paid.

DESIGN DECISION — whose budget is it, when one meter runs many questions?

A price charges one meter for the whole workload, so the caller's `budget_cents` is
the budget of one question's loop: the loop is handed it on top of what the meter
already holds, or the second question would be judged against the first one's
spending. A question whose budget buys no round at all answered nothing and cost
nothing — a price is not a promise that every question was looked at.

DESIGN DECISION — what does a price over no questions answer?

Two rows of zeros, a rollup of `None` cents per answer rather than a division by
nothing, no charges at all in the meter, and an empty `where_it_lost`. `worth_it`
on those rows is `"within-noise"`: the checked pipeline neither cost more nor
covered more, which is exactly what a comparison of nothing to nothing says.

TODO: implement `BASELINE_KEYS`, `ROLLUP_KEYS`, `MIN_WORTH_IT_GAIN_BP`, `price`,
`rollup`, `where_it_lost` and `worth_it`.
"""

import stage_01
import stage_03
import stage_07
import stage_08

BASELINE_KEYS = ("kind", "cost_cents", "answered", "hit_bp")
ROLLUP_KEYS = ("cost_cents", "answered", "cents_per_answer", "delta_cents",
               "delta_answered")
MIN_WORTH_IT_GAIN_BP = 400


def price(index, corpus, meter, questions, limit, budget_cents, round_cap):
    """Both rows over one question set, the naive pipeline first and the checked second.

    Each row is a `BASELINE_KEYS` record: its `kind`, the cents the meter charged
    while that row ran, how many questions it answered, and the share of every
    expected id it brought to the customer, in basis points. The meter is never
    reset — a row's cost is its own delta — and the tick of a question's charges is
    its position in `questions`. A `questions` that is not a tuple of question
    records, or a `limit` that is not a count of hits, is refused by name. The
    budget is one question's, and a question whose budget buys no round at all
    answered nothing.
    """
    raise NotImplementedError("stage 9: implement price()")


def rollup(rows):
    """The two `BASELINE_KEYS` rows added up, in `ROLLUP_KEYS` order.

    `cost_cents` and `answered` are the two rows' sums; `cents_per_answer` is what
    one answer cost over both rows and `None` when nothing was answered at all;
    `delta_cents` and `delta_answered` are the checked row's minus the naive one's.
    Anything but exactly the two rows of a price, naive first, is refused by name.
    """
    raise NotImplementedError("stage 9: implement rollup()")


def where_it_lost(index, corpus, meter, questions, limit, budget_cents, round_cap):
    """The qids the checked pipeline paid more for and answered no better.

    One entry per question, in the questions' own order: the checked row charged
    more cents for it than the naive row did, and its answers brought the customer
    no more of the question's expected ids than the naive row's retrieved hits did.
    Priced the way `price` prices both rows, against the meter it was handed.
    """
    raise NotImplementedError("stage 9: implement where_it_lost()")


def worth_it(rows):
    """The verdict on the checked row against the naive one.

    `"within-noise"` when the checked row's `hit_bp` is within
    `MIN_WORTH_IT_GAIN_BP` of the naive one's either way; `"worth-it"` when it is at
    least that much better *and* answered no fewer questions; `"not-worth-it"`
    otherwise.
    """
    raise NotImplementedError("stage 9: implement worth_it()")

"""Agentic Retrieval From Scratch — stage 10: Which stage failed, and whether the checker beat the baseline.

Nine stages of a pipeline that checks itself, and this one holds the whole thing
against the only two records that are not the course's own. The customer's old
pipeline failed on twelve questions and left a row for each one: the chunk ids
it produced for the document, the hits it ranked, how many it kept, what it
cited, whether its answer was right — and, in the last field, the customer's own
verdict about which stage failed. That last field is the whole temptation of a
debugger. A row that already says *chunk* lets `diagnose` agree with the customer
every time by reading the answer off the answer, and a debugger that agrees with
a label it was handed has checked nothing at all.

So this stage never reads it. `diagnose` decides from the evidence, in the
pipeline's own order, and the first thing true of a row is its verdict: an
answer that was right failed nowhere; a document whose clause index holds
clauses the failure's chunks lacks failed in the chunker; a question stage 5
would itself call ambiguous whose expected clauses all failed to come back
failed in the rewriter; an expected clause that never came back failed in
retrieval; one that came back below the kept line failed in the reranker; one
that was kept and never cited failed in grounding; and everything else is the
answer itself. Only `agreement` reads the customer's label, and what it answers
is a number: how many diagnoses the customer's own record confirms, and which of
them it does not.

The other half of the stage is the checker's own report, and it is a number
rather than a mood. `eval_checker` runs the checked loop over the customer's
questions with the naive retrieval beside it: how many questions came back with
an answer, how much of what the questions expected those answers actually cited,
how much of what they cited was never expected at all, which abstentions were
right because the pipeline could not have answered, and what the whole
evaluation cost on the meter it was handed. The verdict is held against the
naive baseline and behind a sample floor, because a difference of a few hundred
basis points over four answers is not evidence of anything.

    DIAGNOSIS_KEYS               the three fields of a diagnosis, in order
    FAILURE_STAGES               the closed vocabulary a diagnosis is spelled in
    EVAL_KEYS                    the six fields of the checker's report, in order
    EVAL_MIN_SAMPLE              how many answers a verdict has to stand on
    EVAL_MIN_GAIN_BP             how many basis points of coverage it has to be
    diagnose(corpus, failure)    -> DIAGNOSIS_KEYS, from the evidence alone
    distribution(diagnoses)      -> the counts, the fids by stage and the worst
    agreement(diagnoses, corpus) -> how many the customer's own labels confirm
    eval_checker(index, corpus, questions, meter, limit, budget_cents, round_cap)
                                 -> EVAL_KEYS, the checker's report and its verdict

DESIGN DECISION — why does the debugger read the evidence instead of the label?
Because the label is the thing being checked. The customer's twelve rows carry
their own verdict, and a debugger that answered with it would agree with the
customer every time and in every case, which is exactly what makes it worthless:
the label is ground truth, and holding a rule against ground truth is the only
way to learn whether the rule is right. Reading it would also throw away the
reason — which clause was dropped, which expected id never came back, at which
rank it came back — and the reason is the whole product of a debugger. The label
is read in one place and one place only, `agreement`, and there it is compared
with rather than obeyed.

DESIGN DECISION — why does the tree decide by first match rather than by
weighing the evidence?
Because the pipeline is a sequence and the faults are nested rather than
independent. A clause the chunker never produced cannot be retrieved, cannot be
reranked and cannot be cited; a clause that was never retrieved cannot be
reranked either. The evidence in one row is therefore true of several stages at
once, and the only honest verdict is the earliest stage that could have
caused what the row shows. `FAILURE_STAGES` is ordered the way the pipeline
runs — chunk, rewrite, retrieve, rerank, ground, answer — so the tree walks the
evidence in the order the customer's own pipeline walks a question, and the
first thing true of the row is its answer. The one branch that is not read off
the row's raw fields is `rewrite`, and it is not this stage's opinion either: it
is stage 5's own `ambiguous`, asked about the customer's own question, so the
debugger and the rewriter cannot disagree about whether a question was ambiguous
in the first place.

DESIGN DECISION — why is `none` in the vocabulary at all?
Because a labelled failure set is not a set of failures. A row can sit in the
customer's file with an answer that was right — the pipeline got there the hard
way, or the question was re-asked later — and the honest verdict for it is that
no stage failed. It is the first branch of the tree and it short-circuits: there
is nothing to diagnose in a row whose answer was right, so the debugger never
asks the library anything about it, and a debugger that did would be a debugger
that reads a document's whole clause index to decide that nothing is wrong.
`none` is a verdict and never a failing stage, which is why `distribution`
reports it in the counts and never in `worst`.

DESIGN DECISION — why does the worst stage break ties in the vocabulary's own
order?
Because "which stage failed most" stops being a question with one answer the
moment two stages fail equally often, and the answer has to be a function of the
run rather than of how a dictionary happened to be built. `FAILURE_STAGES` is
already ordered by the pipeline, so the earliest stage of the tie wins: the
faults are nested, so the earlier stage is the one that caused the later one,
and a reader who re-runs the report gets the same name for the same row set.
A stage with no failures at all is still the answer when every count is zero —
the tie is total, and the vocabulary's order settles it — and `none` never
enters the comparison, however many rows it accounts for, because a stage that
did not fail is not an answer to "which stage failed".

DESIGN DECISION — why does the checker's verdict sit behind a sample floor?
Because a coverage difference in basis points is only as good as the number of
answers standing under it. A pipeline that answers one question perfectly and
abstains on fifteen has a coverage of ten thousand basis points and has told the
customer nothing about whether checking itself was worth it. `EVAL_MIN_SAMPLE`
is that floor and `EVAL_MIN_GAIN_BP` is the same noise bound the reranker and
the cost comparison already use, so the checker cannot bless a pipeline on a
difference the rest of the course would call noise — and it cannot call that
pipeline better than the naive one either, since beating the baseline is a claim
about answers and not about a ratio.

this file: the first-match diagnosis tree over the customer's own evidence and
never over their label, the distribution that names the worst failing stage,
the agreement that holds the two records against each other, and the checker's

"""

import meter
import stage_03
import stage_05
import stage_08

DIAGNOSIS_KEYS = ("fid", "stage", "reason")

FAILURE_STAGES = ("chunk", "rewrite", "retrieve", "rerank", "ground", "answer",

EVAL_KEYS = ("answered", "hit_bp", "unsupported_bp", "abstained_correctly",

EVAL_MIN_SAMPLE = 4

EVAL_MIN_GAIN_BP = 400

    """

    raise NotImplementedError("stage 10: implement distribution()")

    """How many of these diagnoses the customer's own labels confirm.

    `agree` the count, `disagree` a sorted tuple of the fids that differ, and

    """
    raise NotImplementedError("stage 10: implement agreement()")

    """The checker's own report, and its verdict against the naive baseline.

    `unsupported_bp` the share of citations that were not expected,
    `abstained_correctly` the abstentions on questions whose expected ids were

    """

files.codecraft/api.py:
"""The tiny API an authored course uses to describe its stages.

A course is a directory containing `course.py`:

    from codecraft.api import stage

    TITLE = "Build a Bloom Filter"
    DESCRIPTION = "A probabilistic set, from hashing to false-positive math."

    def check_1():
        from bloom import BloomFilter
        bf = BloomFilter(bits=64, hashes=2)
        bf.add("x")
        assert "x" in bf
        assert "y" not in bf, "a fresh filter must not report false members"

    STAGES = [
        stage(
            1,
            file="bloom.py",
            title="add and contains",
            tags=["hashing", "data-structure"],
            action="Implement add() to set the k bit positions.",
            predict="can contains() ever be certain an item is absent?",
            hints=["bits = bits[:] to avoid shared state",
                   "use one hash salt per position"],
            check=check_1,
        ),
        ...
    ]

`codecraft run <course>` imports this file, runs each `check`, records the
attempt, and hands the result to the adaptive engine. `hints` are optional —
when omitted, the engine generates them from `action`/`predict`.
"""

from dataclasses import dataclass, field
from typing import Callable, Dict, List, Optional


@dataclass
class Stage:
    id: int
    file: str
    title: str
    check: Callable[[], None]
    tags: List[str] = field(default_factory=list)
    action: str = ""
    predict: str = ""
    hints: List[str] = field(default_factory=list)
    solution: Optional[str] = None   # e.g. "solutions/bloom.py: BloomFilter.add"

    def meta(self) -> Dict[str, object]:
        return {
            "file": self.file,
            "title": self.title,
            "tags": list(self.tags),
            "action": self.action,
            "predict": self.predict,
            "hints": list(self.hints),
            "solution": self.solution,
        }


def stage(id: int, file: str, title: str, check: Callable[[], None],
          tags: Optional[List[str]] = None, action: str = "", predict: str = "",
          hints: Optional[List[str]] = None,
          solution: Optional[str] = None) -> Stage:
    """Convenience constructor so course.py stays readable."""
    return Stage(
        id=id, file=file, title=title, check=check, tags=list(tags or []),
        action=action, predict=predict, hints=list(hints or []),
        solution=solution,
    )
